definition: The smallest particle of an element that retains the chemical properties of that element. Made up of a nucleus containing protons and neutrons, surrounded by electrons.
The tiny, dense, positively charged centre of an atom containing protons and neutrons.
A positively charged particle found in the nucleus. Relative mass 1, relative charge +1.
A neutral particle found in the nucleus. Relative mass 1, relative charge 0.
A negatively charged particle that orbits the nucleus in shells. Relative mass very small, relative charge −1.
The number of protons in the nucleus of an atom. Determines which element it is. Also called proton number.
The total number of protons and neutrons in the nucleus of an atom.
Atoms of the same element with the same number of protons but different numbers of neutrons — so they have the same atomic number but different mass numbers.
An early model of the atom proposed by J.J. Thomson, suggesting the atom was a ball of positive charge with electrons embedded in it like plums in a pudding.

The alpha particle scattering experiment that disproved the plum pudding model — most particles passed through but some were deflected or bounced back, showing the nucleus is tiny, dense and positive.
The model of the atom proposed by Rutherford — a tiny, dense, positively charged nucleus at the centre surrounded by electrons.
An improved atomic model where electrons orbit the nucleus in fixed energy levels or shells.
The spontaneous and random emission of radiation from an unstable nucleus as it tries to become more stable.
Radioactive decay is spontaneous — it is not triggered by external conditions such as temperature or pressure.
Radioactive decay is random — it is impossible to predict exactly when a particular nucleus will decay.
A particle emitted in alpha decay, consisting of 2 protons and 2 neutrons (same as a helium nucleus). Has charge +2, stopped by a few cm of air or a sheet of paper.
A fast-moving electron emitted from the nucleus when a neutron turns into a proton. Has charge −1, stopped by a few mm of aluminium.
High-frequency electromagnetic radiation emitted from an unstable nucleus. No charge, no mass, stopped by several cm of lead or thick concrete.
The process by which radiation removes electrons from atoms, creating ions. Alpha particles are the most ionising; gamma rays are the least.
The ability of radiation to pass through materials. Alpha has the least penetrating power; gamma has the most.
Low-level radiation present everywhere in the environment from natural sources (rocks, cosmic rays, radon gas) and artificial sources (medical, nuclear industry).
The time taken for half the radioactive nuclei in a sample to decay. Also the time for the activity of a source to halve.
The number of nuclear decays per second from a radioactive source. Measured in becquerels (Bq).
The unit of radioactive activity. 1 becquerel = 1 decay per second.
When radioactive material is deposited on or inside a person or object — the source of radiation is on or in the body.
When an object is exposed to radiation from an external source but the radioactive material is not on or in the object.
The splitting of a large, unstable nucleus (e.g. uranium-235) into two smaller nuclei, releasing energy and neutrons. Used in nuclear power stations.
In nuclear fission, neutrons released by one fission reaction go on to trigger further fission reactions, releasing more neutrons and energy in a self-sustaining process.
The joining of two small nuclei to form a larger nucleus, releasing large amounts of energy. Occurs in stars. Requires extremely high temperatures and pressures.
Some unstable nuclei decay by emitting a neutron, reducing the mass number by 1 without changing the atomic number.
